abstract: Adaptive threat responses require accurate appraisal of danger signals and flexible behavioral control. Anxiety and trauma-related disorders are marked by avoidance that outlasts the circumstances warranting it, yet such states rarely arise from genetic or environmental insult alone. Here we show that the two converge on a defined prefrontal population by releasing the TSC complex's constitutive brake on mTORC1. Using activity-dependent genetic targeting in mice, we accessed medial prefrontal cortex neurons recruited during the early phase of social isolation - a population projecting predominantly to the lateral septum - and deleted Tsc2 selectively within them. Ensemble-specific Tsc2 haploinsufficiency suppressed autophagic flux without altering bulk translation and produced behavioral avoidance that was rapid and efficient yet no longer under stimulus control, escalating into extra-CS epochs and generalizing to a novel, non-reinforced context. Mutant animals bypassed the phase in which freezing and shuttling compete, and in vivo calcium fiber photometry revealed ensembles locked to the cue but unable to signal trial outcome or track the competing Pavlovian response. Reinstating restraint on mTORC1 through ensemble-restricted Raptor knockdown or systemic Rapamycin restored stimulus control over avoidance, whereas Tsc2 haploinsufficiency in mPFC neurons without social isolation produced no phenotype. These findings identify TSC-restrained, mTORC1-dependent proteostasis within stress-recruited ensembles as a gene-by-environment locus for maladaptive avoidance. More broadly, they suggest that excessive avoidance in anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorders may arise not from genetic risk or adversity alone but from their convergence on mTORC1 signaling cascade.
